segments.caption: Every probability distribution a data scientist needs, in one video.
What each one looks like, when to use it, and the Python code. Save this one!
To choose, ask one question: what am I measuring?
Counting things: how many? Measuring things: how long, or how much?
Or testing a result?
Bernoulli.
One single try, with two outcomes: yes or no.
A coin flip. Will this customer buy? Is this email spam?
Binomial.
The number of yeses in a fixed number of tries.
Heads in ten flips. Buyers out of a hundred visitors.
Geometric.
The number of tries until the first success.
Calls until the first sale. Rolls until the first six.
Poisson.
How many events happen in a stretch of time.
Calls per hour. Website visits per minute. Typos per page.
Uniform.
Every outcome is equally likely.
A fair dice roll. A random number generator.
Normal.
The bell curve: values cluster around an average.
Heights. Exam scores. Measurement errors.
Exponential.
The waiting time until the next event.
Time between customers. Time until a machine fails.
Log-normal.
Positive values with a long right tail, from growth that multiplies.
Incomes. House prices. Stock prices.
Pareto.
A few giants hold most of the total: the eighty twenty rule.
Wealth. City sizes. Sales per product.
The t-distribution.
Like the bell curve, but with fatter tails, for small samples.
Averages from just a few values, and t-tests.
Chi-square.
Checks whether counts match what you expected.
Is this dice fair? Are two categories related?
And a bonus: bimodal.
Two humps usually mean two groups mixed together.
Like restaurant orders, with a lunch rush and a dinner rush. Split the groups first!
Using them in practice takes three steps.
Plot a histogram of your data, and match its shape to these cards.
Then fit it in Python, and check the fit with a Q-Q plot.
